summary: This unit teaches you to choose, check and use electrical and electronic measuring instruments safely and accurately: voltage indicators, multimeters, clamp meters, insulation and continuity testers, earth electrode testers, RCD and loop testers, oscilloscopes and thermal cameras. You will learn how instruments work, how good a reading is, how to carry out and interpret the main installation tests, how to find faults with measurements, and how to keep instruments calibrated and results properly recorded.

blocks.p: Every decision an electrician makes about safety rests on a measurement: 'this circuit is dead', 'this insulation is sound', 'this earth path is good enough to trip the breaker'. A wrong instrument, a wrong setting, a damaged lead or a misread display can turn that decision into an accident. At Level 3 you choose the instrument for the job, plan the tests, take and interpret the readings, check others' results, look after the team's instruments and report what you find.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Choose instruments with the right measurement category, check leads and probes, and prove dead with a proved two-pole tester.
Understand how a reading is made
Explain input resistance, ghost voltages, RMS and true RMS, resolution and accuracy, and work out the possible error in a reading.
Pick the instrument and setting that will give a safe, useful reading for each job.
Test continuity of protective conductors, insulation resistance and polarity in the right order, and judge the results.
Understand live tests and earth testing
Test an earth electrode; explain earth fault loop impedance and RCD/GFCI tests and who may do them.
Use clamp meters, leakage clamps, oscilloscopes and thermal cameras correctly.
Use voltage, voltage drop and resistance readings to locate open circuits, poor joints and insulation faults.
Keep them in calibration, check them between calibrations, replace fuses correctly and store them well.
Record results so they can be traced, report failures in writing, and stop unsafe use of instruments by others.

blocks.note: In Jamaica you will meet both US (NEC) and British/IEC terms and instruments: ground and earth, GFCI and RCD, equipment grounding conductor and protective conductor. Many test instruments sold here follow the IEC standards. This kit gives both terms; your instructor will tell you which test tables and limits the Centre uses.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Live tests (such as earth fault loop impedance and RCD trip time) are done only by competent, authorised people. As a trainee you do dead tests, under supervision, on circuits that are isolated and proved dead.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Instrument safety: categories, leads and safe isolation

blocks.p: A voltage spike on the supply, for example from lightning or a large motor switching, can be several thousand volts for a split second. If an instrument cannot withstand it, it can arc internally and explode in your hands. The **measurement category** tells you how big a spike the instrument is built to survive. The closer you work to the supply intake, the bigger the spikes and the higher the category you need.

head: Category
Where
Examples
rows: Service entrance, JPS meter, service drop, main disconnect
Distribution boards, busbars, fixed wiring, permanently connected motors and equipment
Appliances, portable tools, the outlets themselves
Circuits not connected to the mains

ul: Choose at least the category for the place you will work, **and** a voltage rating at least the highest voltage there. For 110/220 V work in distribution boards, CAT III 300 V is the minimum; CAT III 600 V or CAT IV gives more margin.

The **category matters more than the voltage figure**. A meter marked CAT III 600 V is safer in a distribution board than one marked CAT II 1 000 V, because it is built to survive the bigger spikes found there.
The instrument, its leads and its probes all need a suitable rating: the lowest-rated part sets the rating of the whole set.

head: Feature
Why
rows: Stop your fingers sliding onto the metal tips.
Short exposed tips, or retractable shrouds
Less metal to bridge two terminals and cause a short circuit and arc flash. Good practice (as in the UK guidance GS38, widely followed) is no more than about 4 mm of exposed tip, less where possible.
Limit the energy if a lead is shorted.
Cracked or brittle insulation can expose live conductors.
Leads long enough for the job, but not trailing
Over-long leads tangle and catch on things.

flow: Read the label: the function, range, CAT rating and calibration date
Look at the case, display and battery
Check the leads and probes for cracks, cuts and loose tips
Choose the function and range, and plug the leads into the right sockets
Prove it works on a known source or proving unit
Only then connect it to the circuit

blocks.note: **Never measure voltage with the leads in the current (A) sockets.** On the current range a meter has almost no resistance, so across a supply it is a short circuit: the fuse must break a huge current, and if it is the wrong fuse or the meter is damaged, it can explode in an arc flash. Check where the leads are plugged in every time you pick up a meter.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Before any dead test or any work, the circuit is isolated and proved dead. The instrument for proving dead is a **two-pole voltage indicator** (voltage tester), with a matching **proving unit** that gives a known voltage without needing a live circuit.

flow: Identify the circuit from the drawings and labels; warn people
Switch off, lock off with your own padlock, and tag
Prove the tester on the proving unit
Test at the point of work between every pair: line–neutral, line–earth, neutral–earth (and line–line on two-line 220 V circuits)
Prove the tester again on the proving unit
Only then treat the circuit as dead

ul: If the tester fails its second check, the 'dead' result means nothing: get a working tester and repeat the whole test.
A **non-contact voltage detector** ('volt stick') is only a quick warning. It can miss voltage (weak battery, screened or armoured cable, how you hold it), so it can never prove dead.
A multimeter can be used only if it is suitable and you are trained, and its function, range and leads are checked. A two-pole tester has no wrong setting, which is why it is preferred.
If you leave the job and come back, even for an hour, **prove dead again** before touching anything. Someone may have removed a lock, or another supply may have been connected.

sections.title: How meters work and how good a reading is

blocks.p: Connecting an instrument changes the circuit a little. A good instrument changes it so little that the reading is still true.

head: Measuring
Connected
Instrument's own resistance
Why
rows: Very high (often about 10 MΩ for a digital meter)
So it draws almost no current and does not upset the circuit
Very low (a fraction of an ohm)
So it adds almost nothing to the circuit's resistance
Supplies its own small test current
The part must be isolated and disconnected from other paths

blocks.p: **Loading** matters in high-resistance electronic circuits. Example: a 12 V supply feeds two 2 MΩ resistors in series, so each has 6 V across it. A meter with 10 MΩ input across one of them forms 10 MΩ in parallel with 2 MΩ = 1.67 MΩ, so it reads 12 × 1.67 ÷ 3.67 = 5.45 V, not 6 V. In power circuits the effect is too small to matter.

blocks.h: Ghost voltages and the LoZ setting

blocks.p: Because a digital meter draws so little current, it can show a voltage on an isolated cable that has been picked up from live cables running beside it in the same conduit or trunking (by capacitive coupling). This **ghost (phantom) voltage** may read tens of volts but has almost no energy behind it. But a voltage on an 'isolated' cable may also be **real**: the wrong breaker, a second supply, a generator or a borrowed neutral.

ul: Many meters have a **low-impedance (LoZ)** setting, which loads the circuit (often with a few kilohms). A ghost voltage collapses to near zero; a real supply stays at about its normal value.
A two-pole voltage indicator also loads the circuit, so it does not show ghost voltages.
Until you know, **treat the cable as live**. A reading that stays up on LoZ means a real supply: trace and isolate it, then prove dead again, and report the wrong labelling.

blocks.p: An AC voltage rises and falls 50 times a second in Jamaica. Its **RMS** (root mean square) value is the DC value that would give the same heating, and it is the value quoted for supplies and shown by meters: '220 V' means 220 V RMS. For a pure sine wave, **peak = RMS × 1.414**, so 220 V RMS peaks at about 311 V and 110 V RMS at about 156 V. An oscilloscope shows the peaks.

Many cheaper meters are **average-responding**: they measure the average and multiply by a fixed factor that is correct only for a pure sine wave. Drives, computers, LED drivers, UPS units and many inverters draw or produce distorted waveforms (for example a stepped 'modified sine' wave). On these an average-responding meter can be wrong by a large amount, often reading low. A **true-RMS** meter measures the real heating value of any waveform. Use true RMS for modern loads.

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: The smallest step the display can show on a range
On a range showing 199.9, the resolution is 0.1 V
The largest number the display can show
A 3½-digit meter shows up to 1999 (2 000 counts); a 4½-digit meter up to 19999
How close the reading is to the true value

blocks.p: Resolution is **not** accuracy: a meter can show 0.01 V steps and still be 2 V out. Accuracy is usually given as **±(a % of the reading + a number of digits)**, where one digit is one step of the last figure on that range.

**Example.** A meter is ±(0.8% + 3 digits) on a range that reads to 0.1 V, and shows 118.0 V. 0.8% of 118.0 = 0.94 V; 3 digits = 3 × 0.1 = 0.3 V; total ±1.24 V. The true value could be anywhere from about 116.8 V to 119.2 V.

blocks.note: When a reading is close to a pass/fail limit, work out the instrument's possible error. If the limit falls inside the error band, the result is doubtful: retest with a more accurate, recently calibrated instrument, or treat it as a failure until proved otherwise. Two meters that disagree slightly may both be within their accuracy.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Display
Means
In base units
rows: higher than the instrument can show: record exactly what it displays

head: Instrument
Use it for
Do not use it for
rows: Two-pole voltage indicator and proving unit
A quick first warning that a cable may be live
Digital multimeter (true RMS, CAT III or better)
Voltage, current (small), resistance, continuity on electronics and control circuits
Proving dead unless suitable and you are trained; insulation testing
Load current without breaking the circuit
Currents in a cable where line and neutral pass through the jaws together
Small leakage currents (mA), by clamping line and neutral together
Protective conductor continuity, R1 + R2, bonding; reads to 0.01 Ω with a test current of about 200 mA
Insulation between conductors and to earth at 250, 500 or 1 000 V DC
Continuity, insulation, loop impedance, RCD tests in one instrument
Live tests by anyone not competent and authorised
Checking that a fault will trip the protective device fast enough (live test)
Trip current and trip time (live test)
Resistance of an earth rod to the general mass of earth
Live installations with the earth conductor connected
The order of the three phases before connecting a three-phase motor
Seeing waveforms: shape, frequency, distortion, noise
Mains measurements with an ordinary earthed probe clip
True power (W), apparent power (VA), power factor, harmonics
Finding hot joints, overloaded parts and failing bearings, on load
Finding which breaker feeds an outlet without switching off the board
Proving dead: always test after isolating
Quick check of outlet wiring and polarity
Proving dead; it does not find every fault

blocks.h: Choosing a multimeter for a team

ul: **Category and voltage:** at least CAT III for boards and fixed wiring (CAT IV if used at the intake), at a voltage at least as high as the system.
**True RMS**, because so many loads are electronic.
**LoZ setting**, to tell ghost voltages from real ones.
**Fused current ranges**, with high-breaking-capacity fuses, and accuracy and resolution suited to the work.
**Good leads and probes**, a clear display, a tough case, and a calibration certificate. Read the maker's instructions before use.

blocks.note: The instrument that is easiest to grab is not always the right one. Ask: what am I trying to find out, how accurate must it be, is the circuit live or dead, and is this instrument rated for this place?
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Dead tests: continuity, insulation resistance and polarity

blocks.p: A new or altered installation is tested **dead** before it is ever switched on. The order matters: each test proves something that the next depends on, and faults must be found before voltage is applied.

flow: Prepare: drawings, circuit list, instruments in calibration and checked
Isolate, lock off and prove dead
Inspect: terminations, cable support, breaker sizes, damage
Continuity of protective conductors (and bonding)
Insulation resistance
Polarity
Earth electrode, if there is one
Only then: live tests and switch-on by a competent person

ul: Use a low-resistance ohmmeter. First **null (zero) the leads**: touch them together and press the null button, so the leads' own resistance is taken off. If you cannot null them, measure the leads and subtract that figure from every reading.

**R1 + R2 method** for a radial circuit: at the board, link the circuit's line conductor to its protective conductor. At each outlet or light, measure between line and protective conductor. The reading at the far end is the resistance of the line plus the protective conductor, end to end, and it also confirms polarity.

Compare the reading with what the cable should give: resistance per metre (from the table) × length. Example: a table gives 19.5 mΩ per metre for line plus protective conductor; a 30 m circuit should read about 0.0195 × 30 = 0.59 Ω.
Readings rise in proportion to length. A reading much higher than expected (for example double) points to a loose terminal, a poor joint or a wrong connection; a reading of OL means an open circuit.

blocks.p: An insulation resistance tester applies a high DC voltage between conductors, and between conductors and earth, and shows the resistance in megohms. Good insulation reads very high.

head: Circuit (IEC/British test tables)
Test voltage
Minimum
rows: SELV and PELV (extra-low voltage, such as 24 V controls)
Up to 500 V, including 110 V and 220 V circuits

blocks.p: These are the IEC/British figures; the specification or the inspecting authority may set different ones, and your instructor will tell you which the Centre uses. A new circuit normally reads far above the minimum, often hundreds of megohms or above the tester's range.

ul: Disconnect anything that could be damaged by the test voltage or give a false low reading: surge protective devices (SPDs), LED drivers, dimmers, electronic timers and sensors, RCDs with electronics, and equipment plugged in.
Where items cannot be disconnected, **join line and neutral together and test from them to earth**, so there is no test voltage across the electronics.
Remove lamps, and **close every switch**, so the wiring beyond each switch is tested too.
Warn people nearby, and keep your hands off the conductors during the test.
Test line to neutral, line to earth and neutral to earth (and between lines on two-line circuits), as the job requires.

After each test, let the tester **discharge** the circuit before you touch it. A long cable stores charge like a capacitor; most testers discharge it automatically when the button is released, as long as the leads stay connected.
Reconnect everything afterwards, and check it is reconnected.
Compare each reading with the minimum in the specification.
Compare circuits with each other: one circuit far lower than similar ones is suspect, even if it passes.
Longer circuits and circuits with many outlets read lower, because there are more insulation paths in parallel.
The same low reading on every circuit suggests something shared, such as an SPD left connected or a fault on the neutral bar.
A low reading means: isolate, find the cause (for example by splitting the circuit at a midpoint and testing each half), repair and retest. Never energise a circuit that has failed.

blocks.p: Polarity tests check that every single-pole switch, fuse and breaker is in the **line** conductor, that the centre contact of a screw lamp holder is connected to line and the screw shell to neutral, and that outlets are wired correctly (line, neutral and earth to the right terminals). If a switch were in the neutral, the light would go off but the lamp holder would stay live, ready to shock someone changing the lamp. Dead polarity is checked with the R1 + R2 test: with line linked to the protective conductor at the board, a low reading must appear on the terminal that should be line, and only there.

sections.title: Earth electrodes, live tests and protective devices

blocks.p: An **earth electrode tester** measures the resistance between an earth rod and the general mass of the earth, using two test spikes: a **current spike** (C) driven well away from the rod, and a **potential spike** (P) driven in a straight line between them. This is the **fall-of-potential** method.

flow: Plan with the supervisor: the installation must be isolated
Isolate, lock off and prove dead
Disconnect the earthing conductor at the rod's test point, so you measure the rod alone
Drive the current spike well away, in a straight line, at the distance the tester's maker gives
Drive the potential spike about 62% of the way from the rod to the current spike, and read
Move the potential spike about 10% of the distance nearer and further, and read again
If the three readings agree closely, the middle one is the rod's resistance; if not, move the current spike further out and repeat
Record, reconnect the earthing conductor and check it is tight before the supply is restored

ul: Record the readings, the spike distances, the date, the weather and soil condition, and the instrument used.
Soil resistance depends heavily on moisture. After heavy rain a rod reads lower than it will in the dry season; the design must work in the dry season too.

Compare the result with the specification. Under the NEC, a single rod that does not measure 25 Ω or less must be supplemented by another electrode, bonded to it and at least 1.8 m (6 ft) away; the specification may ask for a lower figure.
Never disconnect the earthing conductor of an installation that is in service: a fault at that moment would leave every exposed metal part unprotected.
Clamp-on (stakeless) earth testers can measure some rods without disconnecting them, where there are other earth paths in parallel; follow the maker's instructions for when they give a true reading.

blocks.p: When a line conductor touches earthed metal, the fault current flows round a loop: the supply transformer, the line conductor, the fault, the protective conductor and the earth return. Its total impedance is the **earth fault loop impedance (Zs)**. The lower it is, the bigger the fault current, and the faster the breaker or fuse trips. The designer gives a maximum Zs for each protective device. If the measured value is higher than allowed, a fault may not trip the protection fast enough, and exposed metalwork could stay live long enough to kill. A loop tester also measures the **prospective fault current**, which must not exceed the breaking capacity (kA rating) of the breakers. These tests are done live, by a competent person only.

head: Test
What it shows
rows: The mechanism trips. It does not show at what current or how quickly. Users should press it regularly, as the maker says.
An RCD/GFCI tester (live test by a competent person)

That the device trips at the right leakage current and within the time the standard allows: the **trip time**. For a 30 mA RCD at its rated current the usual limit is 300 ms; GFCIs follow their own standard.
Makes a leak from line to the earth pin. On an outlet with **no earth conductor** it cannot make the leak, so it will not trip the GFCI even when the GFCI is working; use the GFCI's own button there.

blocks.p: Loop impedance, prospective fault current, RCD trip time, live polarity and phase rotation tests need the supply on. They are done only by a competent, authorised person, with the right instrument, leads and PPE, following the safety rules: barriers to keep others away, test leads attached before the supply is touched, one hand where possible, and never on a circuit that has failed its dead tests.

On a three-phase supply the three lines reach their peaks in a set order (the phase sequence). If two lines are swapped, a three-phase motor runs backwards, which can wreck pumps, conveyors and compressors. A **phase rotation tester** checks the order before the motor is connected or after any change to the supply.

ul: A clamp meter measures the magnetic field round a conductor, so it reads current without breaking the circuit.

Clamp **one conductor only**. In a cord or cable, line and neutral carry equal currents in opposite directions; their fields cancel, and the clamp reads almost nothing. Use a line-splitter adaptor for plug-in equipment.
Close the jaws fully and keep the conductor near the centre.
For a small current, wind the conductor through the jaws several times and **divide the reading by the number of turns**.

A **leakage clamp** uses the cancelling on purpose: clamped round line and neutral together (all the live conductors), it reads only the current that is **not** returning through them, which is leakage to earth. Several milliamps suggests a fault or much electronic equipment.

blocks.h: Measuring current with a meter in series

blocks.p: To use a multimeter as an ammeter, the circuit must be **broken** and the meter connected in series, on the right current range and socket. Make and break the connections only with the supply off. Check the range is big enough before switching on, and use this method only on low-energy circuits; use a clamp meter for anything else.
An oscilloscope draws a graph of voltage (up the screen) against time (across it). The screen is divided into squares (divisions).

ul: **Time per division** sets the horizontal scale. Period (one cycle) = number of divisions for one cycle × time per division. Frequency = 1 ÷ period. Example: at 2 ms/div, one cycle covering 10 divisions takes 20 ms, so f = 1 ÷ 0.020 = 50 Hz.
**Volts per division** sets the vertical scale. Example: at 5 V/div, a peak 3 divisions above the centre line is 15 V.
A **×10 probe** divides the signal by 10, so multiply what the screen shows by 10 (unless the scope does it for you).

On an ordinary mains-powered scope, the probe's **earth clip is connected to earth** through the scope. Never clip it to a line conductor: it short-circuits line to earth through the probe. For mains measurements use a differential probe or a suitably rated, isolated instrument.
A thermal camera shows surface temperatures, so it finds joints, breakers, fuses and bearings that are hotter than their neighbours.
The equipment must be carrying its normal load: a poor joint only heats when current flows.
Compare like with like: three similar terminals carrying similar currents should be at similar temperatures. A difference of tens of degrees means trouble.

**Emissivity:** shiny bare metal (bright copper, aluminium, tinned parts) gives off little infrared and reflects other objects, so it reads too cool. Measure painted or insulated parts, or a patch of high-emissivity tape.

Removing a live board cover exposes people to shock and arc flash: only an authorised person does it, with suitable PPE and a barrier, and the cover goes back on straight after. Some boards have infrared windows.

blocks.p: Measurements turn guesswork into fault finding. Work in a logical order, start from what you know is good, and make every test safe.

blocks.h: Voltage readings on a working circuit

blocks.p: On a circuit with the supply on (for example a 24 V training or control circuit), measure across each part with the load switched on:

head: Reading across
If you see about 0 V
If you see the full supply voltage
rows: The contacts are open or burnt: no current is flowing through them
No voltage is reaching it: the break is elsewhere
Voltage is reaching it; if it does not work, the load or its return path is faulty

blocks.h: Tracing a break: keep one probe on the return

blocks.p: Check the meter on a known source. Measure the supply. Then keep the common probe on the supply's return terminal and move the other probe along the circuit, point by point: after the stop button, after the start button (pressed), at the coil. You should see the supply voltage at each point. **The fault lies between the last point with voltage and the first point without it.** Then isolate before any resistance test or repair, repair, retest and record.

A good joint drops only a few millivolts. A joint with extra resistance drops more, and the power lost in it, **P = V × I**, all turns into heat in a small space. Example: 0.6 V across a terminal carrying 20 A gives 0.6 × 20 = 12 W, enough to char insulation and start a fire over time. Such a joint must be isolated and remade.

ul: Continuity: a higher-than-expected R1 + R2 points to a poor joint; test at intermediate points to find which section.

Insulation: if a circuit reads low, split it (open a joint near the middle) and test each half; keep halving until the fault is found. Look first where faults are likely: damp boxes, outdoor fittings, places where cables enter steel boxes or have been nailed or screwed through.
Remember to disconnect electronics, which can look like faults.

blocks.p: If two team members get different readings for the same thing, do not just pick one. Check both instruments (on a check box or known source), both methods (leads nulled? spikes in the same places? the same test voltage?) and the conditions, then repeat the test together.

blocks.note: When the tests show a fault, leave the circuit isolated, locked off and labelled, and report the fault in writing, even if the customer wants it switched on today. Explain why. A circuit that has failed a safety test is not switched on to please anyone.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Calibration** compares an instrument with a more accurate reference, traceable to national standards, and records (and if needed adjusts) its errors. It is done by a calibration laboratory at the interval set by the maker or the company, often every 12 months, and sooner if the instrument is dropped, damaged or gives doubtful readings. A **calibration label** on the instrument shows when the next calibration is due, and the certificate is kept on file.

blocks.h: Setting up a system for the team

ul: Keep a **register** of every instrument: type, serial number, who holds it, the last calibration date and the next due date.
Label each instrument with its due date. An instrument past its date is withdrawn until it is calibrated; use an in-date one instead.

Between calibrations, check testers regularly (for example weekly) on a **check box** of known resistances, or against a reference meter, and log the results. A reading outside the maker's stated accuracy means: withdraw it, label it, send it for calibration.
Prove voltage indicators on their proving unit before and after every use.
Inspect leads and probes before every use; take damaged ones out of service at once.

If an instrument is found to be inaccurate, review the results it gave since its last good check, and retest any that could have been wrong (for example readings close to a limit). The register and serial numbers on the test records make this possible.
Store them clean and dry in their cases. Do not leave them in a closed van in the Jamaican sun: heat damages batteries, displays and electronics.
Remove batteries from instruments stored for a long time; carry spares.

Replace a blown fuse only with the **type, rating, voltage rating and breaking capacity the maker states**. An ordinary glass fuse cannot safely break the huge fault current of a meter connected across a supply, and may burst.
Read the maker's instructions: they give the ranges, accuracy, safe use and limits of each instrument.

blocks.p: Test results are recorded on a **schedule of test results** (or the Centre's test sheet): each reading against its circuit number, with the instrument's serial number, the date and the tester's name. Then any reading can be traced and checked again later, and if an instrument is later found faulty, the results it affected can be found.

ul: A test report gives: the customer and address, the date, who tested, the instruments (with serial numbers and calibration dates), what was tested, the schedule of results, and clear findings with how urgent each is.
A dangerous result (such as low insulation) is left isolated and labelled, explained to the customer, and recommended for repair before use.
A missing safety feature (such as no RCD or GFCI where one is now expected) is recorded as a recommendation, with the risk explained.
The report is signed, a copy is kept, and the customer is advised on the repairs.

blocks.p: As a Level 3, you are responsible for how your team uses instruments. If you see a trainee about to test with cracked leads, the wrong category of meter, leads in the wrong sockets or a tester that has not been proved, **stop the test**, take the faulty item out of use, report it, and show the trainee the right way. Check their readings and sign the schedule only when you are satisfied.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can choose an instrument with a suitable CAT rating and explain why category matters more than the voltage figure.
I can check an instrument, its leads and probes before use.
I can prove dead with a two-pole tester and proving unit, and say why a non-contact detector cannot.
I can explain input resistance, meter loading and ghost voltages, and use a LoZ setting.
I can explain RMS, peak and true RMS, and when true RMS is needed.
I can tell resolution from accuracy and work out the limits of a reading.
I can choose the right instrument for each measurement.
I can carry out continuity, insulation and polarity tests in the right order and judge the results.
I can prepare a circuit with electronics for an insulation test.
I can test an earth electrode with two spikes and judge whether the result can be trusted.
I can explain loop impedance and RCD/GFCI tests and who may do them.
I can use a clamp meter and leakage clamp correctly.
I can read time and voltage from an oscilloscope and use it safely.
I can use a thermal camera and allow for emissivity.
I can find a fault with voltage, voltage-drop and resistance readings.
I can keep instruments calibrated, checked, stored and fused correctly.
I can record results so they can be traced, and report failures in writing.
I can stop unsafe instrument use by others and show the right way.

terms: Accuracy
How close a reading is to the true value, often given as ±(% of reading + digits).
Calibration
Comparing an instrument with a traceable reference and recording or correcting its errors.
Check box
A box of known resistances used to check testers between calibrations.
Earth electrode tester
An instrument that measures the resistance between an earth rod and the general mass of the earth.
Earth fault loop impedance (Zs)
The impedance of the path a fault current takes; it decides how fast the protection trips.
Emissivity
How well a surface gives off infrared; shiny metal has a low emissivity.
Ghost (phantom) voltage
A voltage shown on a dead cable by a high-impedance meter, picked up from live cables nearby.
Insulation resistance
The resistance of insulation between conductors and to earth, measured in megohms with a DC test voltage.
Leakage clamp
A sensitive clamp meter that reads leakage current by clamping all live conductors together.
LoZ
A low-impedance meter setting that makes ghost voltages collapse.
Measurement category (CAT)
A rating that shows the size of voltage spikes an instrument can survive, by place of use.
Null
To zero a continuity tester's leads so their resistance is not included in readings.
Oscilloscope
An instrument that draws a graph of voltage against time.
Polarity
Correct connection of line, neutral and earth, with switches and protective devices in the line.
Proving unit
A device that gives a known voltage to check a voltage indicator before and after use.
R1 + R2
The resistance of a circuit's line conductor plus its protective conductor, end to end.
Resolution
The smallest step a display can show on a range.
RMS
Root mean square: the AC value with the same heating effect as the same DC value.
Schedule of test results
The record of each test reading against its circuit, with the instrument and tester.
Trip time
How long an RCD or GFCI takes to open after a fault current is applied.
True RMS
A meter type that measures the real RMS value of any waveform, not just a pure sine wave.

c1.title: Dead tests at a new Duncans bakery
c1.text: Odane, a Level 3 electrician, leads the dead tests on a new bakery in Duncans, Trelawny, before it is switched on. The board has eight final circuits, including 220 V oven circuits and LED lighting with drivers, a surge protective device (SPD) connected inside the board, and a 24 V SELV control circuit for the proving cabinet. The cable table gives 19.5 mΩ per metre for line plus protective conductor on the outlet circuits.

c2.title: An unexpected reading at a Cross Roads office
c2.text: Trainee Shanoya has isolated and locked off a lighting circuit at an office in Cross Roads, Kingston. Her multimeter shows 46 V between line and earth at the light; on the meter's LoZ setting it still shows 108 V. The office also has an inverter that feeds its computers, and on its output an older meter reads 96 V while a true-RMS meter reads 112 V. Some old two-wire outlets, with no earth conductor, are protected by a GFCI outlet upstream.

c3.title: Testing an earth rod at a Siloah farmhouse
c3.text: At a farmhouse in Siloah, St Elizabeth, Devon tests the building's single earth rod with an earth electrode tester and two spikes, after the installation has been isolated and the earthing conductor disconnected at the rod. The current spike is 30 m from the rod. With the potential spike at 18.6 m he reads 38.6 Ω; 3 m nearer the rod, 37.9 Ω; 3 m further away, 39.4 Ω. It has rained heavily for a week. The specification follows the NEC rule for a single rod.

c4.title: A hot breaker at a Balaclava hardware store
c4.text: During a thermal-imaging survey at a hardware store in Balaclava, St Elizabeth, the load terminal of the 30 A breaker feeding the air-conditioner shows 68 °C, while similar terminals are about 38 °C. The air-conditioner is drawing 24 A, and there is 0.9 V across the terminal joint. The busbars are bright, unpainted copper. A trainee clamps a meter round the air-conditioner's two-core flexible cord and reads 0.02 A.

c5.title: The instrument register at a Buff Bay contractor
c5.text: A contractor in Buff Bay, Portland, keeps a register of its test instruments. At its annual calibration, one insulation tester was found to read 8% high; its last good calibration was 12 months earlier. The weekly check-box log shows another tester reading 0.91 MΩ on the 1.00 MΩ check resistor, where its maker states ±5% accuracy. A helper has replaced a multimeter's blown 10 A fuse with an ordinary glass fuse of the same amp rating.

questions.q: With the SPD still connected, every circuit reads about 0.6 MΩ from line and neutral to earth. What is the best next step?
o: Record 0.6 MΩ, as it is the same on every circuit
Disconnect the SPD as its maker says, then retest
Raise the test voltage to 1 000 V for a truer reading
Fail every circuit, and search each one for faults
questions.why: The same low reading on every circuit points to something they share: here the SPD, connected between the supply conductors and earth. SPDs and electronics give false low readings and can be damaged by the test voltage, so they are disconnected (or line and neutral are joined and tested to earth), the circuits are retested, and the SPD is reconnected afterwards.

questions.q: Under the IEC test tables, which insulation test voltage suits the 24 V SELV control circuit?
o: 250 V DC
500 V DC
1 000 V DC
24 V AC
questions.why: SELV and PELV circuits are tested at 250 V DC (minimum 0.5 MΩ); circuits up to 500 V, such as 110 V and 220 V, at 500 V DC (minimum 1 MΩ); and higher-voltage circuits at 1 000 V DC. Disconnect any electronics on the control circuit first. An insulation test always uses DC.

questions.q: Outlet circuit 5 is 40 m long and reads 0.80 Ω for R1 + R2 after the leads are nulled. What does this show?
o: It is about double the expected value: suspect a joint
It is far too low, so suspect a short between conductors
It is close to the 0.78 Ω expected, so it is acceptable
Any reading under 1 Ω passes, whatever the cable length
questions.why: Expected R1 + R2 = 0.0195 × 40 = 0.78 Ω, and 0.80 Ω is within a few per cent, which normal variation and temperature explain. A reading much higher than expected would point to a poor joint. There is no fixed '1 Ω' pass mark: the right value depends on the cable and its length.

questions.q: On the LoZ setting the reading stays at 108 V. What does this tell Shanoya?
o: It is a ghost voltage, so the circuit can be worked on
The meter is faulty, as two settings gave two readings
It is induced voltage, which LoZ always makes bigger
It is real: treat it as live and find the source
questions.why: A ghost voltage picked up from nearby cables has almost no energy behind it, so it collapses when the LoZ setting loads the circuit. A reading that holds near 110 V is a real supply: a wrong breaker, a second feed or a borrowed neutral. Touch nothing, trace and isolate the source, then prove dead again with a proved two-pole tester.

questions.q: Which reading of the inverter's output should Shanoya trust?
o: 112 V on the true-RMS meter
96 V on the older meter
104 V, the average of the two
Neither: only a scope reads AC
questions.why: Many inverters give a stepped 'modified sine' wave. An average-responding meter is calibrated for a pure sine wave and reads other waveforms wrongly; a true-RMS meter measures the real heating value. Use true RMS on inverters, drives, LED drivers and computers.

questions.q: A plug-in GFCI tester will not trip the GFCI from one of the old two-wire outlets it protects, but the GFCI's own TEST button does trip it. Why?
o: The GFCI is faulty and must be replaced before anyone uses it
Two-wire outlets cannot be protected by a GFCI at all
The tester needs an earth path, and the outlet has none
The plug-in tester works only on 220 V GFCI outlets
questions.why: A plug-in tester makes its test leak from line to the earth pin. With no earth at the outlet, no current leaks, so the GFCI has nothing to detect. The TEST button makes a leak inside the device, which needs no earth. Such outlets should be labelled as GFCI-protected with no equipment earth.

questions.q: Why was the potential spike placed at 18.6 m?
o: It is half-way, so the two spikes balance each other out
At about 62% of the way to the current spike, it reads true
Any distance works; the tester corrects for it automatically
It keeps the spike away from the house's water pipes
questions.why: In the fall-of-potential method, a potential spike about 62% of the way from the rod to the current spike, in a straight line, gives the rod's true resistance in even soil. Readings about 10% of the distance nearer and further away check that the spikes are far enough apart.

questions.q: What do Devon's three readings tell him?
o: They differ, so the current spike must be moved further out
They are all under 50 Ω, so the rod has passed
They are too close together to mean anything at all
They agree closely, so about 38.6 Ω can be trusted
questions.why: The readings are within about 2% of the middle one, so the spikes were far enough apart and 38.6 Ω is the rod's resistance. Had they differed widely, the current spike would need moving further out. Whether 38.6 Ω passes is a separate question, answered by the specification.

questions.q: Under the NEC rule the specification follows, what should happen with this single rod?
o: Add a second electrode, bonded, at least 1.8 m away
Pass it, since the three readings agreed with each other
Water the soil round the rod, then test it again
Fit a smaller main breaker so faults trip sooner
questions.why: The NEC requires a single rod that does not measure 25 Ω or less to be supplemented by another electrode, bonded to it and at least 1.8 m (6 ft) away. Agreement between the readings shows the test was valid, not that the rod passes. Watering the soil only hides the problem for a few days.

questions.q: Why should Devon record that it had rained heavily all week?
o: Rain makes the tester read high, so the result should be lowered
Rain only matters for rods driven less than 1 m into the ground
Wet soil lowers the reading; in the dry season it may be higher
The weather must be written down, but it has no effect on results
questions.why: Soil resistance depends heavily on moisture, so a rod tested after a week of rain usually reads lower than it will in the dry season, when it must still work. Recording the weather and soil condition lets later results be compared fairly; the design should allow for the dry-season value.

questions.q: About how much heat is being produced in the faulty terminal joint?
o: About 26.7 W
About 0.04 W
About 518 W
About 21.6 W
questions.why: Power = volts across the joint × current through it = 0.9 × 24 = 21.6 W, all of it heating one small terminal, which is why it is 30 °C hotter than its neighbours. A good joint drops only a few millivolts. It must be isolated, cleaned and remade to the right torque, and the breaker checked for heat damage.

questions.q: Why might the camera show the bright copper busbars as cooler than they really are?
o: Copper carries heat away so quickly that it never gets warm
Bare shiny metal emits little infrared, so it reads low
The busbars carry much less current than the breakers they feed
The camera reads correctly only on black or painted surfaces
questions.why: A thermal camera measures the infrared a surface gives off. Bright metal has a low emissivity: it gives off little infrared and reflects other objects, so it reads cooler than it is. Measure painted or insulated parts, or a patch of high-emissivity tape, and compare like with like.

questions.q: Why did the trainee's clamp meter read only 0.02 A round the two-core cord?
o: The out and return currents cancel: clamp one conductor
The cord's insulation blocks the magnetic field from the jaws
The cord is too thin for the clamp to sense its field
Clamp meters cannot read currents below about 30 A
questions.why: In a cord, line and neutral carry equal currents in opposite directions, so their magnetic fields cancel and the clamp reads almost nothing (a small reading is leakage). Clamp a single conductor, or use a line-splitter adaptor. A leakage clamp uses this cancelling on purpose to measure leakage.

questions.q: The board cover must be off for the camera to see the terminals. Which arrangement is right?
o: Any trainee may do it, if the camera stays 1 m from the board
Switch the board off first, then take the images at once
An authorised person in arc-flash PPE, others kept back
Leave the cover off all day, so the survey can be done slowly
questions.why: Opening a live board exposes everyone near it to shock and arc flash, so only an authorised person does it, with suitable PPE and a barrier keeping others back, and the cover goes back on straight after. Switching off first removes the heat the survey is looking for.

questions.q: What should be done about the insulation readings taken with the tester that read 8% high?
o: Nothing, since the calibration laboratory has now adjusted the tester
Lower all of the past readings by 8% on the old test records
Retest every circuit the company has tested in the past five years
Review results since its last good check; retest those near limits
questions.why: A tester that reads high could have passed insulation that was really below the limit. Find every result taken with it since its last good calibration (the register and serial numbers make this possible), judge which could have been failures, and retest those. Changing old records by a percentage is not acceptable.

questions.q: What should happen to the tester that read 0.91 MΩ on the 1.00 MΩ check resistor?
o: Keep using it, as 9% is close enough for site work
Withdraw it, label it and send it for calibration
Keep using it, but add 9% to all its future readings
Use it only for continuity, not for insulation tests
questions.why: Its error is (0.91 − 1.00) ÷ 1.00 × 100 = −9%, outside the maker's ±5%. It is withdrawn, labelled 'Do not use', recorded in the register and sent for calibration, and its recent results are reviewed. Correcting readings by hand is unreliable and unsafe.

questions.q: Why is the ordinary glass fuse in the multimeter dangerous?
o: It may burst, as it cannot break a big fault current
It will blow too often, which wastes the helper's time
It makes the meter read currents about 10% too high
It is dangerous only if the fuse is a different colour
questions.why: A meter's current-range fuse must break the very large fault current that flows if the meter is wrongly connected across a supply. Makers fit high-breaking-capacity fuses of a stated type, rating and voltage. A glass fuse can explode or keep arcing, turning a slip into an arc flash in the user's hands.

questions.q: An oscilloscope shows the 220 V supply as a sine wave peaking at about 311 V. What should you conclude?
o: The supply is about 40% too high and must be reported
The scope probe is set to the wrong ratio and needs changing
It is normal: 220 V RMS has a peak of about 311 V
The waveform is distorted, so the meter reading is wrong
questions.why: Supply voltages are given as RMS values. For a sine wave, peak = RMS × 1.414, so 220 V RMS peaks at about 311 V (and 110 V at about 156 V). A meter shows the RMS value; a scope shows the actual peaks.

questions.q: Why must you never clip an ordinary oscilloscope probe's earth lead to the line conductor of a mains circuit?
o: The scope would show the waveform upside down and confuse you
The probe only measures DC, so it gives no reading on AC
The earth lead is too thin to carry the circuit's load current
It is earthed through the scope, so it shorts line to earth
questions.why: On a mains-powered scope the probe's earth clip is joined to the scope's earth. Clipped to line, it shorts line to earth through the probe lead, which can flash, burn out the probe and harm the user. Use a differential probe or a suitably rated isolated instrument for mains measurements.

questions.q: A 12 V supply feeds two 1 MΩ resistors in series. A meter with a 10 MΩ input reads 5.71 V across one of them instead of 6 V. Why?
o: The meter is out of calibration and must be withdrawn at once
Its 10 MΩ in parallel lowers the resistance being measured
The supply has dropped from 12 V to about 11.4 V under load
The resistors' tolerance always makes the second one read low
questions.why: The meter's 10 MΩ is in parallel with the 1 MΩ resistor, giving about 0.91 MΩ, so that part of the divider gets less of the 12 V: 12 × 0.91 ÷ 1.91 = 5.71 V. In high-resistance electronic circuits even a good meter loads the circuit; in power circuits the effect is negligible.
